item.title: bAdari-view
item.description: Mīsū 3.1.3 states the view of the anti-Jamini Mīmāmsā philosopher Bādari. On this view, only substances, qualities and purificatory acts are to be considered as being subservient to sacrifice, result and a person. In other words, sacrifice, the result and a person do not become subservient to anything because they do not serve the purpose of anything. By contrast, the triad of substances, etc. render assistance to other things and hence are to be treated as subsidiaries. Under MīSū 3.1.4 Jaimini mentions his own view that even actions are subsidiaries since they serve the purpose of the result by bringing about the latter.

item.title: Jammalamadaka shrInivAsa sangrahaH
item.description:
१

Mīmāṃsā Darśana
Dharma • Language • Action • Reality

What is Mīmāṃsā?

  • Inquiry, investigation, critical examination
  • Primarily: inquiry into the meaning of the Veda
  • Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā: karma-kāṇḍa, dharma, injunction, ritual action
  • Uttara-Mīmāṃsā: Vedānta, jñāna, Brahman

Central Concern

  • dharma-jijñāsā — inquiry into dharma
  • “codanā-lakṣaṇo artha dharmaḥ”
  • Dharma is known through Vedic injunction
  • Not all duty is known through perception alone

Authority of the Veda

  • Veda is apauruṣeya — not authored by a human person
  • It is a unique source for knowing dharma
  • Its authority does not depend on an individual speaker

Philosophy of Language

  • Śabda is central
  • How do words and sentences convey meaning?
    • Abhihitānvayavāda (Bhāṭṭa): words first convey individual meanings, then sentence meaning is formed
    • Anvitābhidhānavāda (Prābhākara): words convey connected meaning within the sentence

Pramāṇas

Pratyakṣa (perception) Anumāna (inference) Upamāna (comparison)
Arthāpatti (postulation) Śabda (verbal testimony) Anupalabdhi (non-apprehension)

Knowledge and Validity

  • Svataḥ-prāmāṇya: cognition is intrinsically valid
  • Invalidity is known later through contradiction or defect

Ontology

  • Reality branches into:
    • Ātman (enduring self, knower, agent, enjoyer)
    • Manas (inner organ)
    • Śarīra & Indriya (body and senses)
    • Dravya, guṇa, karma (substance, quality, action)
    • Sāmānya / Jāti (universals)
    • Abhāva (absence)
    • Śakti (potency or capacity)
    • Apūrva (unseen potency linking action to future result)

Karma and Duty

  • Nitya — obligatory regular action
  • Naimittika — occasional duty
  • Kāmya — action for a desired result
  • Niṣiddha — prohibited action
  • Prāyaścitta — expiatory action
  • Proper action produces consequences; apūrva connects act and result

Vedic Sentence Types

  • Vidhi — injunction
  • Niṣedha — prohibition
  • Mantra
  • Arthavāda — praise / explanation / support
  • Nāmadheya — naming passage

Hermeneutic Tools

  • Śruti, liṅga, vākya, prakaraṇa, sthāna, samakhyā
  • Pradhāna and aṅga
  • Krama (order)
  • Atideśa, ūha, bādha

Mokṣa

  • Release from bondage, pain, and karmic entanglement
  • Not centered on mystical absorption
  • Rooted in right knowledge of duty and right action

Major Schools

A. Bhāṭṭa (Kumārila Bhaṭṭa)

item.title: kumArIla on buddhists
item.description:
Source: TW

Kumarila Bhaṭṭa says the Buddhists are rebellious sons who are ashamed that they can never live up to the achievements of their fathers (the Veda) & hence despise them.

वेदमूलत्वं पुनस् ते तुल्य-कक्ष-मूलत्वाक्षमयैव लज्जया च मातापितृ-द्वेषि-दुष्ट-पुत्रवन् नाभ्युपगच्छन्ति c.f - TV, 195

“I am my father’s son” is probably what Kumarila had in mind, because he clearly lists out how most of the core doctrines of the Buddhists come from the Upanishads, and even their virtue signalling like ahimsa, charity, compassion, equanimity comes from older Aryan scripture.

item.title: ManjushrI sophist summary
item.description:
Source: TW

Old sources

  • Earliest usage of “mīmāṁsā”: “investigating a doubtful point (of a ritual) and arriving at a conclusion thereon.

  • Earliest extant text = Jaimini’s Mīmāmsāsūtra-s (MS).

  • Mīmāṁsākas preceding Jaimini (mentioned in the MS): Bādarāyaṇa (MS 1.1.5; 5.2.19; 6.1.8; 10.8.44; 11.1.65), Bādarī (MS 9.2.33; 6.1.27), Atiśāyana (MS 6.1.6; 3.2.43; 3.4.24), Krşņājini (MS 4.3.17; 6.7.35), Lāvukāyana (MS 6.7.37), Kāmukāyana (MS 11.1.58; 11.1.63), Atreya (MS 4.3.18; 5.2.18; 5.1.26) and, Alekhana (MS 6.5.17)
